title: Respect for Bill and Don Sebesky's praise
summary: Why the records still sound fresh.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: I take it your relations with Bill were, on the whole, pretty good.
I always respected his talent. Bill has, like everybody, problems, but if you can--I don't think I

could work as closely with anybody again, because his work habits and mine are just too different, but that was really the only problem. Intellectually we got along very well; a great respect for his talent, which most people do, I'm not alone in that.
I think probably one of the--a real genius is in there crying to come out; I've always felt that. He should be (inaudible) and not some of the people who are, because they can't cut it.

I think I mentioned this to you--Don Sebesky wrote an arranging book called, The Contemporary Arranger, a few years ago, and he spent a good amount of space just talking about your band and talking about the impact that it had on studio recordings, and he said something to the effect that if you can find any of the Sauter-Finegan records, buy them, because they sound as fresh now as
That's the truth. You know why I think so?

Because they were both written and played with the idea of bringing out a life thing. I think it's that life that sticks with us. It's just something that has to be, at that time. It can sound pretty dull if it's not played right, but it was played very well. It took a lot of effort and a lot of time to do it that way though, you don't walk in and walk out of the studio in three or four hours.
